title: Arthritis Exercise for Beginners: Safe First Steps
meta_title: Arthritis Exercise for Beginners: Safe First Steps
meta_description: Beginner-friendly arthritis exercises to build confidence, movement and strength, with simple pacing tips and signs you should stop and get advice.
excerpt: Beginner-friendly arthritis exercises to build confidence, movement and strength, with simple pacing tips and signs you should stop and get advice.
direct_answer: Start with a manageable activity that suits your joints, balance and energy. Build gradually and use a stable setup for seated exercise. Some osteoarthritis discomfort can occur at first, but severe pain or new joint heat and swelling needs assessment. Ask a physiotherapist for an individual plan and adaptations.
author: Louis Maxwell
keywords: arthritis exercise for beginners, beginner arthritis exercises, low impact exercise
content:
Starting exercise with arthritis does not have to mean joining a class or completing a demanding routine. A useful first step is finding movement you can repeat, at a level that fits your joints, balance and energy. Strength, mobility and general fitness all matter, but you do not need to tackle everything at once.

This guide offers a way to choose your first activity and two seated examples from the NHS. It is general information, not a personalised exercise prescription. Follow any restrictions or programme from your own physiotherapist, surgeon or rheumatology team.

Should you get advice before starting?

If you are unsure whether an exercise is suitable, check with a GP or a health professional involved in your care. This is especially important when you have recent surgery or an injury, frequent falls, or a health condition that affects what you can safely do. Do not use a general beginner routine to work around an unexplained new symptom.

For osteoarthritis, NICE recommends exercise tailored to the person, including muscle strengthening and general aerobic fitness. Supervised sessions may help. A seated routine can be a starting option, but it is not automatically right for every joint problem or a complete long-term programme.

Which activity is a sensible first choice?

Choose something accessible that you do not dread repeating. Low-impact options include walking, cycling, swimming or water-based exercise. If standing or walking is difficult, an appropriate seated exercise may be more manageable. Ask for help choosing an option if pain or balance makes each attempt feel unsafe.

Set a practical goal, such as feeling more confident walking indoors or moving a stiff ankle. Begin with an amount you can manage rather than a class length or step target chosen for someone else. Note how the activity affects both your symptoms and an everyday task that matters to you.

How should you set up for seated exercise?

The NHS sitting-exercise guide recommends a solid, stable chair without wheels. Your feet should rest flat on the floor with knees bent at right angles. Its routine uses a chair without arms so movement is not restricted. If you need armrests to sit safely or get up, ask a physiotherapist for an adapted exercise rather than giving up needed support.

Wear comfortable clothing, clear the space around your feet and keep water nearby. You should be able to control the movement without sliding or feeling unsteady. If gripping the chair hurts your hands, ask for an alternative setup rather than gripping harder.

What are two examples you can try if suitable?

These examples and repetition counts come from the NHS sitting-exercise page, which also has photographs. They are starting references, not a requirement to finish a set through pain. Build slowly and ask for an adaptation if the movement is not comfortable or safe for you.

Seated hip marching

  1. Sit upright without leaning against the chair back, holding the sides of the chair.
  2. Lift one leg with the knee bent, only as far as is comfortable.
  3. Lower the foot with control, then repeat with the other leg.

The NHS example is five lifts with each leg. Do not lean back to lift higher or force a painful hip. If this setup is difficult, pause and ask a physiotherapist for another way to work the relevant muscles.

Seated ankle movement

  1. Sit upright and hold the side of the chair. Straighten one leg with the foot off the floor.
  2. Point the toes away, then bring them back towards you.
  3. Repeat with the other foot, keeping the movement controlled.

The NHS example suggests two sets of five stretches with each foot. If holding the leg up or straightening the knee is uncomfortable, do not force it. A clinician can suggest a supported alternative. Use the linked NHS photographs rather than guessing from the exercise name.

How can you build up without overdoing it?

Repeat a manageable amount before making it harder. The NHS sitting routine suggests aiming for at least twice a week and gradually increasing repetitions. Your own plan may differ. There is no need to make every session longer because the calendar says another week has passed.

Make one small change at a time, such as a few more comfortable repetitions or a little longer at the same easy activity. Keep a brief note of what you did and how you felt afterwards and the following day. If the change repeatedly leaves you struggling with normal tasks, step back and ask for advice about the dose or exercise choice.

Over time, ask how to include suitable strengthening and general fitness alongside mobility. Simply repeating a seated movement does not necessarily cover every part of your exercise needs.

Does pain mean you should stop?

Not all discomfort means harm. NICE explains that osteoarthritis pain may initially increase when therapeutic exercise begins, but regular, consistent exercise can improve pain, function and quality of life over time. That does not mean pushing through severe pain or treating all swelling as a normal response.

For rheumatoid arthritis, the NHS living-with guide advises stopping and resting if a particular activity causes severe pain or makes the joints warm and swollen. If an activity repeatedly triggers a flare, find an alternative with advice from your team. Balance rest with suitable movement rather than treating a painful day as a test of willpower.

Which symptoms need urgent advice instead of exercise?

Ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 for sudden severe pain and swelling in one joint, a hot or red joint, or joint pain with feeling hot, cold or shivery. Redness may be harder to see on brown or black skin. A serious joint infection can occur without a fever. Do not try to exercise a newly hot swollen joint to see whether it loosens up.

Use urgent care rather than waiting for your next physiotherapy session. In England, Scotland and Wales, call 111 when appropriate; in Northern Ireland, use your GP or GP out-of-hours service. For a life-threatening emergency, call 999.

What should you ask a physiotherapist?

  • Which movements and strengthening exercises fit my joints and other conditions?
  • How much should I start with, and how should I adjust it on a difficult day?
  • What discomfort is expected for me, and what changes mean I should stop or seek help?
  • Can the setup be changed for painful hands, poor balance or difficulty getting out of a chair?
  • How will we review whether the plan is helping the activities I want to do?

Key takeaways

  • Choose a manageable activity and build gradually rather than chasing someone else's target.
  • Use a stable setup and get help adapting movements that are painful or unsafe.
  • Some early osteoarthritis discomfort can occur, but severe pain or new warmth and swelling needs a different response.
  • A newly hot, swollen or suddenly very painful joint needs urgent assessment, not an exercise experiment.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a gym?

No. Suitable walking or home-based movement can be a starting point. The right choice depends on your joints, safety and goals.

Is sitting exercise enough on its own?

It can help you begin, but a long-term plan may also need specific strengthening, balance work or general fitness. Ask what is missing from your current routine.

Must I complete every repetition?

No. The NHS counts are examples, not a reason to force a painful movement. Build slowly and ask for an adaptation when needed.

Should I stop arthritis medicines when I start exercising?

No. Exercise does not replace prescribed disease-controlling treatment. Discuss medicine changes with your treating team.

Can I follow this after joint surgery?

Follow the surgeon or physiotherapist's postoperative plan and restrictions instead. A general routine is not a substitute for rehabilitation instructions.

Your next step

Choose one suitable activity, check the setup and decide what you want it to help you do. If uncertainty about pain, balance or another condition is stopping you, bring those questions to a physiotherapist rather than abandoning movement or forcing a routine.
